D- Of fields (vv. 16-25) 16"And if a man shall sanctify unto the LORD some part of a field of his possession, then thy estimation shall be according to the seed thereof: an homer of barley seed shall be valued at fifty shekels of silver. 17 If he sanctify his field from the year of jubile, according to thy estimation it shall stand. 18 But if he sanctify his field after the jubile, then the priest shall reckon unto him the money according to the years that remain, even unto the year of the jubile, and it shall be abated from thy estimation. 19 And if he that sanctified the field will in any wise redeem it, then he shall add the fifth part of the money of thy estimation unto it, and it shall be assured to him. 20 And if he will not redeem the field, or if he have sold the field to another man, it shall not be redeemed any more. 21 But the field, when it goeth out in the jubile, shall be holy unto the LORD, as a field devoted; the possession thereof shall be the priest's. 22 And if a man sanctify unto the LORD a field which he hath bought, which is not of the fields of his possession; 23 Then the priest shall reckon unto him the worth of thy estimation, even unto the year of the jubile: and he shall give thine estimation in that day, as a holy thing unto the LORD.

24 "In the year of the jubile the field shall return unto him of whom it was bought, even to him to whom the possession of the land did belong. 25 And all thy estimations shall be according to the shekel of the sanctuary: twenty gerahs shall be the shekel."
Homer: equal to ten ephahs, and the ephah equals 22.9 liters.
If a person vows a part of his field that he inherited from his fathers, the priest values it so that it may be sold to any person who wishes to buy it, and the price is offered to the Temple.

The price is determined according to the amount of seed sufficient for sowing it. An homer of barley seed was valued at fifty shekels of silver, so one calculates how much the land needs, that is, how many homers of seed.
If a person vows a part of his field in the year of jubile, the priest values the price of the field, it is sold to whoever wishes to buy it, and the price is paid to the house of God.

The preceding case in (v. 17) is a vow in the year of jubile. But if a field is vowed after the year of jubile, the priest values its price, and it is less, since years have passed from which the buyer did not benefit, and fewer than 49 years remain until the year of jubile, in which the field will return to God and the priest will receive it (v. 20). The buyer pays the price to the priest; this is the value of the vow, and he works the land and takes its produce until the year of jubile.

If the one who vowed desires the field that he vowed to God and wishes to redeem it for himself, he pays a price greater than its sale price that the priest set, by an amount of a fifth, as happened in the case of the beast and the house (vv. 13, 15).

If the owner of the field does not redeem his field for himself by paying its price with the addition of a fifth, and the priest sold it to any person, then in the year of jubile the field returns to God and the priest receives it to oversee its cultivation and harvest, and it does not return to its owner but becomes holy, that is, set apart for God.

This means that in this case the Law encourages the owner of the field, who was in some difficulty and made a vow to God that He might resolve it for him, that after he has pronounced the vow and before the priest sells the field to any person, he or one of his relatives should hasten to redeem the field and return it to its owner, so that he may hold fast to the inheritance of the fathers, which is a symbol of the eternal inheritance.

Hold fast to the teachings of the Church, the commandments of your parents, and every good thing you have learned, for it is the true inheritance from the fathers that guarantees you the way of life with God.

If a person buys a field from another, and he will of course return it to its owner in the year of jubile, and then vows it to God during the period of his ownership of this field and his enjoyment of its produce, he gives the price of the produce until the year of jubile to the house of the Lord; this is the fulfillment of the vow. The valuation of the field's price until the year of jubile is according to the valuation of the priest, who is the voice of God and just in his judgments. In the year of jubile the field returns to its original owner, from whom the maker of the vow bought it, so that every person may keep the inheritance of his fathers and the portion of every tribe may remain fixed.
Gerah: equal to the weight of a carob seed, or 0.75 of a gram.

God admonishes Moses and all the priests after him that the unit of valuation is to be the shekel of the sanctuary, which equals twenty gerahs, that is, about 15 grams. The meaning is that the unit of valuation should be exact, to ensure a just and precise valuation.

Here he affirms the law of offering the firstborn of animals to God, that is, the first offspring of an animal. It is not right to vow this to Him, because it already belongs to God and must be offered to the Temple. All this concerns clean animals such as the ox and the sheep.

Be careful to offer to God the firstfruits of your day, beginning with prayer before any other work. Would that you join prayer with reading the Holy Bible, choosing a verse to memorize and repeat throughout the day and try to apply in your life. And know that a spiritual beginning with God will give you peace throughout the day and keep you from the snares of the devil.
The firstborn of all animals must be offered to God, but unclean animals such as the donkey may not be offered to the Temple, so in this case one of these things is done:
1- The animal is sold and the price is given to the Temple.
2- If the owner of the animal loves to keep it, this means that he has a desire to possess, so he pays its price, a fifth is added to it, and it is offered to the priests.
3- The animal is redeemed with a lamb, as the Book of Exodus mentions (Ex 13:13).

God used to command the devoting to destruction of some wicked and dangerous peoples because of the multitude of their evils. These had to be put to death and could not be redeemed, as He commanded the devoting of the Canaanite peoples when Joshua entered to possess the land, and he fought them and killed them (Deut 7:1-4; Josh 9, 10, 11). God also commanded the devoting of some persons, even if they were kings, such as Agag king of Amalek, whom the prophet Samuel killed (1 Sam 15:32, 33). As for animals and possessions such as silver and gold, devoting them means offering them to the Lord, and they cannot be sold or redeemed. Whoever transgresses this law brings God's great anger upon himself, as happened with Achan the son of Carmi, who took possessions from Jericho that had to be devoted to God, and God commanded that he be put to death (Josh 7:25). That is, the devoting comes by the command of God or by the judgment of the judges according to the Law.

Obey the guidance of your father of confession by cutting off everything that leads to sin, however precious and dear it is in your eyes or however much your soul desires it, for your salvation is more important than anything in life.

God commanded the offering of tithes from all the produce of the land and of the animals. Here he speaks of the tithes of the produce of the field, which are the grains and all the products of the planted crops, in addition to the tithes of the fruit of the trees, and these are offered to God every year. The produce of the field was offered after threshing, that is, it was offered as grain, and the fruit was either offered fresh, or the grapes could be offered as juice and the olives as oil, which is easy to store without spoiling. The produce of the field was offered in the Temple of God (Deut 12:11), and if it was far from them in the land of Canaan, it could be sold and its price offered in Jerusalem (Deut 14:24-27). Of these tithes the priests, the Levites, the poor and the needy would eat, because the priests and the Levites had no portion in the land like the other tribes.

The tithes of the third year were offered by each person in his own city to the poor and the Levites (Deut 14:28, 29). The seventh year had no tithes because the land is not sown in it, and likewise the year of jubile, that is, the fiftieth year.

Tithes were known among men before their appearance in the Law of Moses, for Abraham offered tithes of the spoils he had taken in his war with the kings to Melchizedek (Gen 14:20). And Jacob vowed to offer tithes to God when He appeared to him on the ladder (Gen 28:22).
If a person desires to keep the tenth of his produce, which he ought to have offered to God, he must pay its price to the Temple and add a fifth to the price, because of his love for material things.

As for the tithes of animals, each year they would gather the young born among them and pass them one by one through a narrow gate, while the shepherd counted with his rod, and when he reached the tenth he took it and offered it to God.

The tenth of the animals is offered without examination, and if its owner finds it good and fat, it is not right for him to exchange it for a weak one, for this is a kind of theft directed against God. If he exchanges it, he is obliged to offer the good animal and also the weak animal that he put in its place, that is, to offer two animals, that is, the fifth, because of the sin of the love of money and the sin of theft. And even if he exchanged the weak tenth animal for a good animal, he offers both as well, so that the Law would not give anyone an opportunity to deceive and exchange the animal for any personal purpose.
He concludes this chapter, and indeed the whole Book of Leviticus, affirming that what precedes is the Law that God gave to Moses at Mount Sinai in the tabernacle of meeting (ch. 1:1).

The blessing of offering tithes is very great, for it is an expression of your love for God. He has no need of material things, but He rejoices in your love for Him and your care for the needs of the Church and of all the needy. God is not indebted to anyone, and He will bless you, as He promised, with heavenly blessings beyond what you imagine.
